classification.difficultyReason: Recall the chord-gradient terminology and put the two function values in subtraction order with the denominator supplied.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a)–(c) directly assess the terminology and difference quotient covered by average-rate-of-change.
questions.methodNote: No separate teaching pages were supplied. The embedded definition and completion scaffold identify average rate of change as change in y divided by change in x, equal to the gradient of the chord.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate change in quantity per unit time into final-minus-initial notation and identify the missing endpoint term in each position.

questions.mappingNote: Each part applies the average-rate-of-change definition to a time-dependent quantity; no numerical calculation or graph method is required.
questions.methodNote: No separate teaching pages were supplied. The question's own scaffolds express average rate as change in quantity divided by change in time, with both changes taken as final minus initial.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate elapsed-time phrases into interval endpoints and generalise that the nth minute starts one minute before t=n.

questions.mappingNote: Identifying interval endpoints supports average-rate-of-change calculations. This is the closest supplied skill; average speed from a graph is not directly assessed.
questions.methodNote: No separate teaching pages were supplied. The task uses elapsed-time endpoints: the nth minute runs from n−1 to n, while the first n minutes run from 0 to n.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied interval endpoints to evaluate the volume model, then apply the taught difference quotient with the correct units. The first interval is scaffolded and the second repeats the method independently.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) supplies the endpoint volumes for (b); (c) applies the same method to a new interval.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Endpoint evaluation followed by the difference quotient is inferred from the explicit task.

classification.difficultyReason: Students translate the time phrases into intervals and calculate two average rates. The hardest part uses the hint and the zero volume at two minutes to explain the physical limit of the model.

questions.mappingNote: The two initial intervals share the volume model; the final part explains its time domain. The printed hint remains visible.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Endpoint differences and physical interpretation are inferred from the task.

classification.difficultyReason: Students identify years zero and five as the endpoints and apply the average-rate formula directly to the supplied exponential model.

questions.mappingNote: The exponential model supplies both endpoint values; the key establishes two-decimal currency precision.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Use the change in modelled value divided by the five-year interval.

classification.difficultyReason: Each part supplies the function and both endpoints. Students apply the same difference quotient throughout, with routine exact arithmetic for the fractions and surds.

questions.mappingNote: All six exact calculations share the printed instruction. The three-column grid retains row order a, b, c, then d, e, f.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Substitute interval endpoints into each function and divide the change in y by the change in x.

classification.difficultyReason: Students use the stated annual compounding to find the ending balance, then subtract the initial investment and divide the gain by four to obtain dollars per year.

questions.mappingNote: The embedded definition remains in the question. Explicit annual compounding and dollar-per-year units resolve the interpretation supported by the keyed monetary answer.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Annual compound growth followed by change in value divided by elapsed years is inferred from the task and confirmed by the key.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine the two distances and the two times, then divide the totals to find the whole-trip speed.

questions.mappingNote: Average-rate-of-change is the closest catalogue skill: this task uses numerical journey data rather than the graph required by average-speed-distance-time.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Combine the journey distances and times before division.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate the rates over the two stated intervals, choose a known distance from which to estimate the distance at five seconds, and use the proximity of the readings to explain which estimate is likely to be more accurate.

questions.mappingNote: Retain the original task and all table values, including x. Record the competing anchor interpretations rather than silently selecting one.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. The key implies applying a wider-interval average rate from t=4 or t=6, whereas interpolation between the specified endpoints is also consistent with the stem.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate the quadratic at the two stated inputs and divide the change in function value by the change in input.

questions.mappingNote: The quadratic and the two x-values fully specify the calculation independently of preceding questions.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Evaluate the function at both endpoints and use the difference quotient.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate the distance model at the interval endpoints and divide each distance increase by its elapsed time. All three parts use the same procedure.

questions.mappingNote: Each of the three printed time intervals maps to its own response leaf, retaining the source three-column arrangement.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. Solutions use change in distance divided by elapsed time.

classification.difficultyReason: Students turn a given average rate into an equation for an unknown endpoint, simplify the quadratic difference quotient and justify that the resulting endpoint is valid.

questions.mappingNote: The whole printed question owns one response, including the requested calculation-based justification.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. Set the difference quotient equal to the stated average rate, solve for the endpoint and check.

classification.difficultyReason: Students interpret the first k minutes as the interval from 0 to k, set the average volume rate equal to 10 and solve the linear equation after cancellation.

questions.mappingNote: The printed seconds/minutes inconsistency is corrected to minutes in accordance with the supplied editorial resolution.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. Use the average volume rate over the interval from 0 to k.

classification.difficultyReason: The supplied intervals guide the calculations. The hardest step is explaining why average rates over shrinking intervals approach the instantaneous rate at the fixed endpoint.

questions.mappingNote: Both printed parts remain in source order. The supplied definition remains visible in part b and is not hidden in its answer.
questions.methodNote: No separate teaching pages were supplied. The question itself defines instantaneous rate and uses successively shorter intervals to motivate the limiting relationship.

classification.difficultyReason: Students convert both speeds into vertical rises, choose a distance at the shared endpoint or an equivalent starting point, and construct a distance–time graph that satisfies both secant constraints.

questions.mappingNote: The source provides no axes or grid. Student construction space is blank; the example graph is answer-only.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. Construct a distance–time graph whose changes in distance are 20 m and 28 m over the two two-second intervals; verify the secant gradients.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert each average speed to a displacement change, account for the shared interval, and explain why smooth, increasing motion still allows different average speeds over the final interval.

questions.mappingNote: The source's two bulleted givens and smooth, increasing condition remain visible. The independent answer records underdetermination rather than silently assuming extra motion conditions.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. Convert each interval average to a displacement difference and test whether the requested difference is determined.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall basic limit facts and method names from sentence cues, including whether the function value must exist.

questions.mappingNote: The limit component of the secant-limit skill is the closest catalogue match. Part (d) also identifies the simplification method used in Question 2.
questions.methodNote: The printed activity identifies the approached coordinate, distinguishes the limit from the function value, and prompts direct substitution or simplification before substitution.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the cued reciprocal trend and transfer it to two denominators that grow without bound.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied secant-limit skill is the closest catalogue match for interpreting and evaluating limits. This question assesses reciprocal limits at infinity.
questions.methodNote: Part (a) supplies the growing-denominator reasoning. Part (b) applies it to a square root and to a power with positive exponent.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the prescribed substitution directly, including at the endpoint of the square root's real domain.

questions.mappingNote: The limit-evaluation component of the secant-limit skill is the closest catalogue match for direct substitution in these four expressions.
questions.methodNote: The printed stem explicitly requires direct substitution. The worked answer to (d) makes the approach from within the real domain explicit while retaining the source notation in the prompt.

classification.difficultyReason: Diagnose the zero denominator, then recognise a difference of squares and cancel the common factor before applying the cued substitution.

questions.mappingNote: Part (b) directly assesses simplifying an algebraic fraction by factorisation. The two parts use the same limit and preserve the failed substitution followed by the successful method.
questions.methodNote: The printed parts explicitly require trying substitution, then simplifying before substituting. The difference of squares exposes the common factor, which can be cancelled for $x\ne1$.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a factorisation that exposes the cancelling factor before substitution. The quartic requires recognising x²−1 as a factor by treating x⁴ as (x²)².

questions.mappingNote: The ten parts use common factors, differences of squares or quadratic factorisation. Part (e) takes a limit in h with x fixed.
questions.methodNote: The printed stem requires simplifying first. Factor and cancel where the original fraction is defined, then substitute in the simplified expression.

classification.difficultyReason: The hint identifies which expression to rationalise. Choose its conjugate, recognise the resulting x−1 factor and cancel before substituting.

questions.mappingNote: Multiplying by the conjugate produces the common factor x−1. The algebraic-fraction skill is the closest available catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: The printed hint directs students to rationalise the denominator.

classification.difficultyReason: The hint directs numerator rationalisation. Apply the conjugate to the whole quotient, recognise that the numerator reduces to x² and cancel it while retaining the conjugate in the denominator.

questions.mappingNote: Conjugate multiplication gives a difference of squares and exposes the common factor x². The algebraic-fraction skill is the closest available catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: The printed hint directs students to rationalise the numerator.

classification.difficultyReason: Decide without a hint to combine the inner fractions, then recognise that 2−x is the negative of the outer denominator and retain the sign through cancellation and substitution.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed algebra is subtracting and simplifying algebraic fractions. The exact teaching sequence lacks independent source evidence.
questions.methodNote: The authored method combines the numerator fractions over 2x, then cancels before substitution.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the substitution from part (a) in the supplied quotient, expand the numerator, cancel the common factor of h and evaluate the limit at the fixed point.

questions.mappingNote: Part (b) directly evaluates the secant-gradient limit for the quadratic at x=1.
questions.methodNote: The printed ‘Hence’ links the substitution in part (a) to the difference quotient in part (b). Expand, cancel h and take the limit.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand the quadratic difference at general x, then use that result to factor and cancel h and establish the stated limit while treating x as fixed.

questions.mappingNote: Part (b) establishes the difference-quotient limit at a general x. The secant-limit skill is the closest available catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: The printed subtitle specifies first principles. Part (a) expands the numerator for use in the limit in part (b).

classification.difficultyReason: Use the given horizontal increment to complete the second point and write rise over run, then identify what happens as the separation decreases.

questions.mappingNote: Part a names the secant; b supplies its second point; c applies change in output divided by change in input; d identifies the increment; e describes the points approaching.
questions.methodNote: No separate teaching pages were supplied. The question itself establishes the secant through P(x,f(x)) and Q(x+h,f(x+h)), followed by its difference quotient and a decreasing increment magnitude.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete the supplied reasoning from secant gradient to tangent gradient and connect the limiting quotient with the derivative function.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c establish tangent and secant terminology; d–e complete the limiting difference quotient; f identifies the derivative and its output; g names differentiation by first principles. No numerical or graphical method has been substituted.
questions.methodNote: No separate teaching pages were supplied. The question itself develops the tangent as a limiting secant, then defines its gradient through the first-principles limit and names the derivative function.

classification.difficultyReason: Build the secant gradient from the two points, simplify to the stated expression and interpret its limit as a tangent gradient. The diagram and part sequence guide the transitions.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced directly assessed task interprets the limiting secant gradient as the tangent gradient.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. The question explicitly scaffolds coordinates, secant gradient and its limit.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand the shifted square, factor the numerator to cancel h before taking the limit, and identify the resulting value as the tangent gradient at x=1.

questions.mappingNote: The question evaluates a limiting secant gradient at x=1 and identifies its tangent meaning.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Follow the printed expansion, quotient, limit and geometric-interpretation sequence.

classification.difficultyReason: Students form and simplify the secant gradient from the supplied endpoints, then interpret its limit as the tangent gradient. The parts cue each stage.

questions.mappingNote: The final part interprets the limit as the tangent gradient at x=1.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Calculate the secant gradient from the printed endpoints and take its limit.

classification.difficultyReason: The quotient is supplied. The quadratic parts require substituting x+h, expanding and subtracting f(x), then factoring out h before cancellation. The follow-up explicitly directs students to take the limit and evaluate the derivative at x=1 for the tangent gradient.

questions.mappingNote: This assesses the algebraic difference-quotient stage of first-principles differentiation.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Substitute into the printed difference quotient, expand, subtract and cancel h for h nonzero.

classification.difficultyReason: The method is named, but students must set up and simplify the quadratic difference quotient, take its limit to obtain a derivative function, and evaluate that function at x = 2.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess quadratic differentiation from first principles and tangent-gradient evaluation.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. The printed instruction explicitly requires first principles: expand f(x+h), subtract f(x), divide by nonzero h, take the limit, then evaluate at x=2.

classification.difficultyReason: Students construct a moving point, infer the limiting secant gradient from the graph and verify the same value with a first-principles quotient at x=2. The prompt directs each transition.

questions.mappingNote: Verification of the derivative at a point is the most advanced task. The preceding parts assess the limit of secant gradients as the tangent gradient.
questions.methodNote: The source prompts specify a slider, a graphical secant estimate and an algebraic first-principles verification.

classification.difficultyReason: Students reuse the requested cubic expansion with a=x and b=h, cancel the constant term and factor h out of the numerator before evaluating the limit.

questions.mappingNote: Expanding the cubic supplies the terms of the difference quotient for the assessed derivative.
questions.methodNote: The source asks for the cubic expansion first and explicitly directs students to use it to differentiate from first principles.

classification.difficultyReason: Part (c) cues the conjugate method, but students must first combine reciprocal radicals to expose a radical difference, track its reversed sign and then cancel h before taking the limit.

questions.mappingNote: The final part applies the first-principles method to a reciprocal square root.
questions.methodNote: The supplied difference quotient and the request for a similar technique establish the use of a conjugate to cancel h before taking the limit.

classification.difficultyReason: Students combine two fractions to prove the supplied difference identity, then divide by h, cancel and take the limit. The intermediate identity and final derivative are both given.

questions.mappingNote: The reciprocal-function identity is the intermediate step in the assessed first-principles derivative.
questions.methodNote: The source supplies the target identity for the difference. Use a common denominator, then divide by h and take the limit.

classification.difficultyReason: The stems cue each differentiation rule and ask for direct recall of notation and the derivative value that gives the tangent gradient.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (b) and (c) directly assess the constant-multiple and sum/difference rules, and part (a) directly assesses the power rule.
questions.methodNote: The printed cloze stems identify the power, constant-multiple and sum/difference rules, derivative notation and evaluation for tangent gradient. No separate teaching pages were supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: The clozes supply the sequence for both lines. The student recalls which values to evaluate, the point-gradient formula and the negative-reciprocal relationship.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied catalogue has no tangent-and-normal equation skill. The power rule is the closest exercise-context match for the differentiation step that starts the procedure.
questions.methodNote: The question supplies the sequence of differentiating, evaluating the derivative and function, using point-gradient form, then using perpendicular gradients at the same point of contact. No separate teaching pages were supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: The student interprets the given zero gradient, identifies the perpendicular as vertical and writes its equation from the given x-coordinate.

questions.mappingNote: The closest supplied skill is derivative-constant-linear because the assessed relationship is between zero gradient and a horizontal tangent line.
questions.methodNote: The printed parts connect zero derivative to a horizontal tangent and ask for the perpendicular normal through the point of contact. No separate teaching pages were supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: After recalling three derivatives, the student identifies the change in coefficient and exponent and generalises both changes to a formula for positive integer powers.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) asks for three recalled results and part (b) asks for a conjecture from those results. The preceding exercise was not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Recall the three derivative results from the previous exercise and infer a pattern for positive integer powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Rewrite a reciprocal radical using a negative fractional exponent, apply the supplied power rule, and express the resulting negative power in an equivalent form.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a)–(g) cover positive, negative and fractional powers. Part (h) tests the constant case.
questions.methodNote: The embedded rule directs students to use index laws to rewrite reciprocals and radicals and then differentiate powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Differentiate polynomial terms already in power form, carrying their coefficients and signs through the supplied rules.

questions.methodNote: Teaching pages unavailable. The parts establish the point and the gradients before using point–gradient form for each line.

questions.methodNote: Use the zero-gradient criterion, show the derivative is positive on the domain, then corroborate it using graphing software as explicitly requested.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive the tangent at a symbolic point, extract its axis intercepts and recognise that their absolute lengths have a constant product across both branches.

questions.mappingNote: Differentiation of a negative power is the directly assessed catalogue skill that supports both the tangent proof and the intercept-area result.
questions.methodNote: Use substitution, sketch the reciprocal curve, apply the power rule to find the tangent gradient, and use the intercept distances to show the area is invariant. The sketch made in part (b) is extended in part (c).

questions.methodNote: The shared instruction requires the chain rule. Fractional and negative powers put the roots and reciprocals into the power form used in Fundamentals 2.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the chain rule, then explain the undefined endpoint gradient by connecting it to a vertical tangent through the semicircle geometry or one-sided slope behaviour.

classification.difficultyReason: Use a difference of squares in √x to reach the supplied reciprocal form, then combine the outer reciprocal derivative with the inner square-root derivative.

questions.mappingNote: The identity requested in part (a) isolates the composite term for differentiation in part (b).
questions.methodNote: Decompose the rational expression into a linear polynomial and a reciprocal term, then differentiate term by term using the chain rule on the reciprocal.

questions.methodNote: Apply the quotient rule and use the sign of the derivative on each interval of the domain. The assigned teaching evidence is unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Differentiate the radical product, use derivative signs to classify its stationary point, then differentiate again and reject the algebraic candidate outside the domain.

questions.mappingNote: Finding and classifying the stationary point is the closest catalogue match. Part (b) extends the calculation to the second derivative and uses the same domain.
questions.methodNote: Differentiate the radical product, use the sign of the first derivative to classify the stationary point, then check the second-derivative zero against the domain. The assigned teaching evidence is unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive the supplied expression using the product rule, then test the proposed zero against the square-root domain and recognise that the endpoint has no finite derivative.

questions.mappingNote: The main task is deciding whether a proposed solution of the stationary-point equation gives a point on the curve.
questions.methodNote: Apply the product rule, then check whether the candidate derivative zero belongs to the domain and whether the derivative exists at the endpoint. The assigned teaching evidence is unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall which variable changes and match each direction of change to a gradient sign in cued statements.

questions.mappingNote: All four completions directly assess increasing or decreasing behaviour and gradient signs.
questions.methodNote: Relate changes in x and y to the sign of the gradient. Separate teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall derivative notation and associate increasing, decreasing and horizontal behaviour with the corresponding tangent gradient signs.

questions.mappingNote: The four statements assess derivative notation and the signs of tangent gradients.
questions.methodNote: Identify the derivative as the gradient function and interpret positive, negative and zero gradients. Separate teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the prompted sequence from piecewise formulas to function sketches, then transfer branch slopes to the derivative formula and graph while recognising the corners and jump where the derivative is undefined.

questions.mappingNote: Both functions assess graphical construction of a derivative, including excluded join points.
questions.methodNote: Sketch the linear branches, identify their gradients and transfer those gradients to the derivative graph. Separate teaching evidence was not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Read the gradient signs on either side of one minimum, then use the parabola's shape to combine those signs and its horizontal tangent into a rising derivative line.

questions.mappingNote: The graph on page 29 and all four continued parts on page 30 are available and form one complete question.
questions.methodNote: Use the sign of a graph's gradient and its horizontal tangent to sketch the derivative. Separate teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate two horizontal tangents and three sign intervals into a derivative sketch, using the changing steepness of the cubic-shaped curve to place the derivative's minimum between the zeros.

questions.mappingNote: The graphical derivative skill is directly assessed by the final part; the first three parts scaffold its sign and zeros.
questions.methodNote: Read derivative signs from rising and falling graph portions, and derivative zeros from horizontal tangents. Separate teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate slopes and horizontal tangents into derivative signs and zeros, then use flattening tails or asymptotic behaviour to distinguish options with similar sign patterns.

questions.mappingNote: Each original graph owns one letter response. All nine derivative options remain given material in a labelled three-by-three diagram grid.
questions.methodNote: Match gradient signs, horizontal tangents and flattening or asymptotic behaviour. Separate teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate horizontal tangents and gradient signs into derivative zeros and intervals, distinguishing a touch at the stationary inflection from a crossing at the minimum and maintaining the alternating signs across three turning points.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 directly assesses sketching the derivative from a supplied graph. Parts (a)–(c) use constant gradients, (d)–(f) use gradients of parabolas, (g), (h) and (j) use two turning points, (i) distinguishes a stationary inflection from a minimum, and (k)–(l) use three turning points.
questions.methodNote: Read the derivative as the tangent gradient. Locate horizontal tangents, determine the sign of the gradient on each interval and use the change in steepness to shape the derivative. The assigned practice graph and the Exercise 7J key support this graphical method. No teaching pages were supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Work backwards from the gradient graph to recognise a quadratic, then use the derivative’s sign change and zero to identify whether the vertex is a maximum or minimum and locate its x-coordinate.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a) and (b) assess constant signed gradients. Parts (c) and (d) assess how the derivative sign change locates and classifies a stationary point. The assigned catalogue has no dedicated inverse-sketch skill.
questions.methodNote: Read the gradient graph directly. Use constant gradient for straight lines, then use the sign and zero of a nonconstant linear gradient to locate and classify the vertex of a parabola.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct each derivative graph by translating tangent direction and steepness into signed heights. The hardest part combines the semicircle’s restricted domain, its horizontal tangent and its two vertical endpoint tangents to locate the zero and infer opposite unbounded end behaviour.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a) and (b) use stationary points and flattening tails. Part (c) uses negative slopes tending to zero. Parts (d) and (e) use positive slopes tending to zero. Part (f) uses the horizontal tangent at the top and vertical tangents at the two ends of the given domain.
questions.methodNote: Treat the height of the derivative graph as the signed tangent slope of the given function at the same horizontal coordinate.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete scaffolded statements linking instantaneous rate to derivative notation, tangent gradient and the limit of average rates.

questions.mappingNote: The five completions assess the distinction between instantaneous and average rates and the notation, graphical meaning and limit for the instantaneous rate.
questions.methodNote: The exercise connects the instantaneous rate to the derivative at a given time, the tangent gradient and the limit of average rates over shrinking intervals.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose the rate from the stated interval or instant and place the dependent quantity and time variable into the supplied derivative fraction.

questions.mappingNote: The parts choose the kind of rate and identify the quantity and time variable in the derivative.
questions.methodNote: The exercise distinguishes a time interval from a single instant, then expresses differentiation of $Q$ with respect to time in Leibniz notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate increasing, decreasing and zero instantaneous change directly into a positive, negative or zero derivative.

questions.mappingNote: The three parts connect increasing, decreasing and zero instantaneous change to derivative values.
questions.methodNote: Read the sign of $Q'(t_1)$ as the sign of the rate at that instant.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the constant gradient as the rate for a straight line and the derivative at a point as the local rate for a non-linear graph.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) identifies the constant gradient and its meaning. Part (b) identifies the graph type and the derivative used to find the local rate.
questions.methodNote: Use a straight line's constant gradient as its rate of change and evaluate the derivative to find the rate at a chosen point on a curve.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that a straight distance–time segment has one constant gradient for both the interval and any instant.

questions.mappingNote: The question applies both ideas to compare average and instantaneous speeds on a straight distance–time segment.
questions.methodNote: Fundamentals 4(a) on source PDF page 34 links a straight line's gradient to its constant rate of change. Fundamentals 1(d) on the same page links the tangent gradient to the instantaneous rate.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose the interval calculation for average speed and the derivative for instantaneous speed, then use the derivative to explain the change in speed.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a) and (b) directly compare average and instantaneous rates. Part (c) interprets both in the context of the car.
questions.methodNote: Use the change in position divided by elapsed time for average speed on this interval and differentiate position for instantaneous speed.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the derivative established in part (b) to find when the diver is momentarily stationary, then return to the height model and interpret the maximum.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses the interpretation of a derivative as vertical velocity and of zero speed at the turning point. The student page supplies an equation and no plotted graph.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate the height at time zero, differentiate the height, then use the zero derivative to locate and interpret the maximum.

classification.difficultyReason: Differentiate the displacement polynomial, evaluate the signed velocity at the supplied times, then choose scales and plot a smooth curve that shows the negative values and the turn.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a) and (b) construct the derivative table and graph; part (c) states what the derivative represents. The task does not estimate a rate from a supplied graph.
questions.methodNote: Differentiate displacement, evaluate the resulting velocity at each given time and plot the signed values against time.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose the quotient rule to establish the stated derivative, use the supplied sign hint to explain the decrease, and convert signed derivative values to positive loss rates.

questions.mappingNote: The question explicitly connects the sign and magnitude of a derivative to a decreasing physical quantity. The hint gives the method for part (c).
questions.methodNote: Use the quotient rule to obtain the given derivative. Interpret its sign and evaluate its magnitude to find rates of loss.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate halfway to the ground into a height of 50 m, solve for the corresponding time, and compare the resulting decrease rate with half the maximum established at impact.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (c)–(e) assess the derivative as a signed instantaneous rate and its interpretation over the fall. Part (b) supplies the physical interval used in those parts.
questions.methodNote: The question explicitly requests dh/dt. Differentiate the height model, evaluate the derivative at the relevant times and use its negative for the magnitude of the decrease.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish the instant at t = 4 from the interval [3,4] and apply the derivative and difference quotient to their respective parts.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) evaluates the derivative at 4 minutes. Part (b) contrasts it with an average over the interval from 3 to 4 minutes.
questions.methodNote: The exercise asks for the derivative at the specified time and change in area divided by elapsed time over the fourth minute. Teaching pages were unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the sign of the given rate to determine flow direction and when the volume changes from increasing to decreasing, then verify both conditions on the proposed model and select its physically valid zero.

questions.mappingNote: The sign of the rate gives flow direction and volume behaviour in parts (a) and (b). Part (c) checks both supplied conditions, and part (d) uses the verified model.
questions.methodNote: The question calls for interpreting the sign of the derivative, differentiating the proposed volume formula, checking its initial value and solving for zero volume. Teaching pages were unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the amount melted into remaining mass, solve for the corresponding time, then evaluate and interpret the signed derivative as a rate of mass loss.

questions.mappingNote: Part (b) gives the time directly, part (c) determines it from the remaining mass, and part (d) compares the magnitude of the mass derivative near the endpoints.
questions.methodNote: Solve the remaining-mass equation for the relevant time, then evaluate the derivative and interpret its sign and magnitude. Teaching pages were unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Use a difference quotient and a derivative to compare two flow rates, then use the decreasing derivative to locate the greatest flow.

questions.mappingNote: Part (c) compares interval and instantaneous rates. Part (d) interprets the decreasing derivative to identify the greatest flow rate.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate the volume at the given times, calculate average rate as change in volume divided by elapsed time, and differentiate for instantaneous flow. Teaching pages were unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish an interval secant and a single tangent from the local change in tangent gradient, then explain why the sign of acceleration remains undetermined.

questions.mappingNote: The task compares an interval average with an instantaneous speed and asks what these rates tell us about how the car is moving.
questions.methodNote: Use the secant gradient for average speed and the tangent gradient for instantaneous speed. No assigned teaching pages were available to verify the source’s treatment.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a speed–time graph with three prescribed regimes and an area of 100 m, then distinguish the speed gained under constant acceleration from the absolute speed.

questions.mappingNote: The graph and numerical parts assess instantaneous speed, average speed and how acceleration changes speed.
questions.methodNote: Represent the three speed regimes on speed–time axes. Use distance over elapsed time for average speed and the gradient of the first segment for constant acceleration. The area under the sketch checks the race distance. No assigned teaching pages were available to verify the source’s treatment of those methods.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the nonnegative amount to bound the model, distinguish the initial zero derivative from the later maximum using derivative signs, and evaluate the cubic at that maximum. The graph and derivative hints cue the approach.

questions.mappingNote: The derivative is interpreted as an instantaneous rate with units and used to determine when the amount increases, decreases and reaches its maximum.
questions.methodNote: Use the printed graph hint to interpret the domain, differentiate the polynomial and use the derivative’s zeros and sign to locate and evaluate the maximum. No assigned teaching pages were available to verify the surrounding examples.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate the secant rate from the endpoints, set the polynomial derivative equal to that rate, and retain both roots by checking the stated closed interval.

questions.mappingNote: Part (b) directly assesses interpreting the derivative as an instantaneous rate and finding when it equals the average rate from part (a). The graph supplies endpoint values and supports the calculation.
questions.methodNote: The assigned evidence contains no teaching pages. The endpoint difference quotient and the equation Q'(t₀)=2 follow from the printed task. Factorising gives both times, including the endpoint allowed by the stated closed interval.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the names for signed position, its rate of change and the rate of change of velocity, with each initial letter supplied.

questions.mappingNote: Identifying acceleration as the rate of change of velocity is the most advanced rate interpretation assessed.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. The printed statements identify displacement as a function of time and ask for the names of its first and second time derivatives.

classification.difficultyReason: Match rightward motion, leftward motion and rest to positive, negative and zero velocity using the supplied initial letters.

questions.mappingNote: The three parts assess what the sign of velocity says about direction and rest.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. The printed directional cues and keyed answers establish the convention that right is positive.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate rest and initial time into zero conditions and express long-term behaviour with limit notation.

questions.mappingNote: Interpreting zero velocity as rest is the closest catalogue fit. The other two parts assess time conventions in the same motion context.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. The stems and key associate rest with zero velocity, initially with zero elapsed time, and eventually with the long-time limit.

classification.difficultyReason: Differentiate a linear displacement and interpret the negative velocity as leftward motion. Recognise that passing through the origin means setting the displacement to zero, then solve the linear equation.

questions.mappingNote: Finding velocity by differentiating the given linear displacement is the directly assessed calculus skill. Its sign gives the direction.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. Fundamentals 1 and 2 on the assigned practice page establish the rate relationship and sign convention. The given formula supports differentiation, direct substitution and solving for time.

classification.difficultyReason: The parts cue direct substitution, polynomial differentiation, interpretation of a negative initial velocity and solution of a linear rest condition.

questions.mappingNote: The velocity-from-displacement skill produces the function used to find initial velocity, starting direction and time at rest.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. The assigned Fundamentals establish the displacement–velocity relationship, the sign convention, and the conditions for initial values and rest. Differentiate the quadratic, evaluate at zero and solve the resulting velocity equation for the time at rest.

classification.difficultyReason: The supplied time columns guide the comparison around the zero of velocity. Students must interpret the unchanged sign to adjudicate the claims and generalise a test for reversal.

questions.mappingNote: The final parts assess whether the sign of velocity changes. Differentiating displacement supplies the velocity needed for that test.
questions.methodNote: Parts (a)–(e) establish the derivative, solve v = 0, and compare signs using the given value table. The key's Q9(a) on PDF page 62 corroborates the sign-table method.

classification.difficultyReason: Students justify the supplied reversal time with velocity signs, distinguish landing from launch, and use the separately cued travel legs to explain why final height differs from total distance.

questions.mappingNote: The final parts directly distinguish the sum of the two distances from the height at the end of the flight.
questions.methodNote: The parts lead from differentiating height and checking the signs of velocity to finding the landing time and adding the distances of the upward and downward legs.

classification.difficultyReason: Without a function or part-by-part cues, students must formulate the procedure, decide which velocity zeros split the interval and specify how absolute position differences combine.

questions.mappingNote: The standalone prompt generalises the distinction between total distance and change in position.
questions.methodNote: The neighbouring practice questions on PDF page 40 show how to check for direction changes and add distances between successive positions.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the maximum found in earlier parts to split the flight into a rise and a fall, then add the magnitudes of the two height changes.

questions.mappingNote: The final part uses both changes in height to obtain total vertical distance. Earlier parts directly assess finding and interpreting velocity.
questions.methodNote: The parts cue substitution for the initial height, differentiation and a sign check for the maximum, and solving height equations to obtain graph points. Total distance uses the rise and fall as in Q4.

classification.difficultyReason: Read direction from the slope at each stated time and identify rest at the three horizontal tangents.

questions.mappingNote: The five time readings assess the sign of an instantaneous rate. Part (b) assesses where that rate is zero.
questions.methodNote: The question requires reading the sign of velocity from the slope of the displacement graph and locating rest at horizontal tangents. Exercise teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Differentiate and check the velocity sign around its zero, then use the established reversal to split the distance travelled and connect the velocity and displacement to the motion description and cubic sketch.

questions.mappingNote: The derivative is needed for rest, reversal and the motion description. The distance and graph also require distinguishing position from distance travelled.
questions.methodNote: Differentiate displacement, find the zero of velocity for non-negative time, check its sign on either side, then add the distances travelled before and after the turn. Use intercepts and the turning point for the graph. Exercise teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct and verify counterexamples that separate zero velocity from reversal, positive velocity from unbounded displacement, and velocity tending to zero from displacement approaching a finite limit.

questions.mappingNote: The counterexamples distinguish a zero of velocity from reversal, positive velocity from unbounded displacement, and velocity tending to zero from displacement tending to a finite limit.
questions.methodNote: Use a displacement function for each counterexample, differentiate it to check the condition on velocity, then verify the direction or displacement behaviour. The printed key supports these checks. Exercise teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Read zero displacement from the intercepts, then use horizontal tangents and positive-gradient intervals for rest and rightward motion. Interpret the steepening positive gradient as increasing speed.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed skill is interpreting instantaneous rate from the displacement graph. Part (a) uses zero displacement, parts (b) and (d) use positive gradient, part (c) uses horizontal tangents, and part (e) uses an increasing positive gradient. Teaching pages were unavailable for checking the exact presentation of this method.
questions.methodNote: Read displacement directly and interpret the sign, zeros and change of gradient as features of velocity. The supplied question graph and matching answer key support this graphical method.

classification.difficultyReason: Match the velocity crests to positions on the displacement graph, then combine velocity signs, turning positions and speed changes to describe the repeating motion.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) reads both initial ordinates. Part (b) finds the first repeated initial displacement. Parts (c) and (d) use the initial velocity sign and the first sign change. Part (e) reads the displacement at the times of the velocity crests. Part (f) combines signed velocity intervals and displacement turning points to describe the cycle. The question itself supports this graphical method.
questions.methodNote: Read positions and times from the paired graphs. Use the sign of velocity for direction and its magnitude for speed.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose to differentiate, identify the actual reversal from the sign of velocity, and split the interval there before summing the absolute changes in position.

questions.mappingNote: The cubic displacement and four-second interval require a direction check before distance can be calculated. The method follows from the assigned question and has no supplied teaching-page verification.
questions.methodNote: Differentiate displacement, check the sign of velocity on either side of the stationary time, then add the distances travelled.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the initial velocity and limiting value to anchor the sketch, then use the positive, decreasing acceleration to show that the velocity rises and levels off.

questions.mappingNote: The given equation is already a velocity law. The central derivative interpretation is acceleration as the rate of change of velocity. The printed Chapter 8 prerequisite remains in source-group evidence.
questions.methodNote: Use the given velocity to calculate the initial value, differentiate to get acceleration, and use the initial value, gradient and limit to draw the graph.

classification.difficultyReason: Differentiate twice, then use the exponential velocity law to sketch its approach to a limiting value and justify why it never reaches zero.

questions.mappingNote: The requested graph and the coming-to-rest question both depend on deriving the velocity law from the given position. Acceleration is needed for the initial value, the graph gradient and the eventual value.
questions.methodNote: Differentiate position to obtain velocity and differentiate again for acceleration. Check the initial values, the sign of velocity and the exponential limits.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose and apply the differentiation rules, test velocity signs to distinguish reversal from initial rest, and compare the eventual signs of velocity and acceleration to decide whether speed decreases.

questions.mappingNote: Each displacement law is a separate motion model. The question distinguishes reversing, tending to rest and slowing down. Two columns preserve the part order while allowing readable fractions and worked responses.
questions.methodNote: Differentiate for velocity, test for sign changes, evaluate displacement and velocity limits, then compare the eventual signs of velocity and acceleration.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert radicals and denominators to fractional or negative indices, then apply the power rule once to each resulting monomial.

questions.mappingNote: All four expressions reduce to single powers. No teaching pages were supplied; the method is inferred from the expressions.
questions.methodNote: Rewrite radicals and quotients as powers, then apply the power rule.

classification.difficultyReason: Set up the required difference quotient, expand and subtract the quadratic expressions, cancel the common factor h, then take the limit.

questions.mappingNote: The instruction explicitly assesses first principles for all four quadratics. The answer key supplies results only; teaching demonstrations were not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Apply the limit definition, expand, cancel, divide by nonzero h, then take the limit.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest part requires dividing each numerator term by x, then differentiating the resulting linear, constant and reciprocal terms separately.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–b use symbolic powers, c–d constant and linear rules, and e–j simplified powers. Teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Use constant, multiple, sum and power rules; rewrite fractions and radicals before differentiating.

questions.mappingNote: All six expressions contain a nontrivial inner function. Part f is printed without y = and remains an expression to differentiate. Teaching examples were not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Apply the chain rule, rewriting reciprocal and radical expressions as powers where appropriate.

questions.methodNote: Apply the product rule with chain-rule derivatives, then factor or combine fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the quotient rule, differentiate the radical denominator in part (d), and clear the nested fraction to simplify the result.

questions.mappingNote: The quotient sequence and answer key support these rules. No source teaching pages were available to verify the demonstrated sequence.
questions.methodNote: Apply the quotient rule; differentiate the radical denominator in part d using the chain rule.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the specified gradient to solve for the point on the curve, then follow the cue in part (b) to form the tangent equation from that point and gradient.

questions.methodNote: Set the derivative equal to the specified gradient, find the point, then use point-gradient form.

classification.difficultyReason: Extract the gradient of the line, take its negative reciprocal, equate that value to the derivative and substitute into the curve to obtain the coordinates.

questions.methodNote: Find the negative reciprocal of the given line's gradient, equate the derivative to it, and substitute into the curve.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert the line gradient to the perpendicular tangent gradient, solve the resulting derivative equation as a quadratic, and recover both points on the curve.

questions.mappingNote: The unknowns are the points at which the tangent has the prescribed gradient.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages are unavailable. The authored solution uses the negative reciprocal of the line gradient, sets the derivative equal to that gradient, and substitutes both roots into the curve.

classification.difficultyReason: Use parallelism to identify the normal gradient, convert it to the tangent gradient to locate the point of contact, then use the normal gradient to form the requested equation.

questions.methodNote: Teaching pages are unavailable. The authored solution uses the parallel normal gradient and perpendicular tangent gradient to find the point, then forms the normal equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate the derivative at the supplied point to obtain the tangent gradient, then substitute the point into the supplied line form to find the intercept.

questions.mappingNote: The task determines the gradient and intercept in the tangent's slope-intercept form.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate the quadratic at each stated interval’s endpoints and divide the change in output by the change in input. All three parts use the same direct procedure.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate the exponential at the two stated endpoints, including the zero exponent, and apply the secant formula once.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish the instantaneous rate at t = 2 from the average rate over the second minute, translate that minute to [1,2], and use the derivative and secant quotient respectively.

questions.mappingNote: The task distinguishes the instantaneous rate at a stated time from the average rate over the preceding interval.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages are unavailable. The authored solution evaluates the derivative at two minutes and uses the endpoint difference quotient over the second minute.

questions.methodNote: The authored solution differentiates the quadratic, sets the tangent gradient to zero at x = 1, and uses the two point conditions to solve for the coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: The composite expression supports the chain-rule classification. Parts (b) and (c) assess a zero and the sign of the derivative.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the sign of the velocity found in part (a) to establish motion in one direction over the first two seconds, then take the difference of the endpoint positions in the correct order.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the given point in the original equation and its zero gradient in the derivative to form and solve two simultaneous equations.

questions.mappingNote: The coordinates supply one equation in the coefficients and stationarity supplies the second.

questions.methodNote: Teaching pages unavailable. The solution uses the derivative sign on both sides of the stationary point and compares function values across it.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the supplied quotient into a labelled secant diagram and explain how its gradient tends to the tangent gradient.
